summary: This document gives guidelines to enterprise administrators on deploying IPv6. Unlike access providers, enterprises face different priorities, such as offering Internet-facing services over IPv6 while still supporting IPv4.

eli5.summary: Companies need to learn a new address language while still using the old one. This RFC offers advice for company network teams about how to roll out IPv6 step by step.

how to deploy ipv6 in an enterprise network

subtitle: A phased playbook for enterprise network teams rolling out IPv6 alongside IPv4.

tldr.problem: Enterprises face different priorities from access providers: they must offer Internet-facing services over IPv6 while still supporting IPv4 for existing networks, devices and applications.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC splits the work into a Preparation and Assessment Phase, an External Phase and an Internal Phase, with security, routing, address planning, tooling and an eventual IPv6-only option covered along the way.
tldr.outcome: It is informational guidance, not a protocol: administrators choose the order of phases to suit their business, with the motto to dual stack when you can and tunnel when you must.

today: RFC 7381 is an Informational document and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. Its advice is guidance for planning, and it notes that several of the documents it relies on were still works in progress in October 2014.

sections.title: Why and How to Phase an Enterprise Rollout
sections.content:
The RFC borrows the definition of an enterprise network from RFC 4057: a network with multiple internal links, one or more router connections to providers, and an actively managed operations team. Its most common driver for IPv6 is that when Internet service providers, including mobile carriers, run out of IPv4 addresses, they provide native IPv6 and non-native IPv4 through technologies such as NAT64, NAT444, Dual-Stack Lite, MAP-T or MAP-E. Native traffic typically performs better and more reliably, so customers reaching an enterprise do better if its public-facing services have IPv6.

The document assumes existing IPv4 networks keep running and that disruption should be minimised by providing native IP wherever possible, which means few flows tunneled, translated or intercepted. It proposes three phases: Preparation and Assessment, External and Internal. The Preparation Phase is highly recommended for everyone. Each administrator decides whether to start with the External Phase or the Internal Phase, because the considerations pull in different directions, for example remote employees whose ISPs provide translated IPv4 that cannot carry the VPN protocols they need.

Even an IPv4-only network needs some care. Internet-facing servers should log the source port number, a reliable timestamp and the transport protocol so that users behind address-sharing technologies can be traced, and rogue IPv6 Router Advertisements can disturb IPv4-only networks.
sections.eli5: You can start by fixing the front door or the rooms inside. Which first depends on who is knocking and what needs help most, but everyone should make a plan before they start.

sections.title: Preparation: Inventory, Training, Routing and Address Plan
sections.content:
Because enabling IPv6 touches the most fundamental Internet protocol, the RFC recommends a professional project manager and an executive sponsor. The inventory has two halves. Network infrastructure is sorted into devices that are already capable, devices that a firmware upgrade can fix and devices that must be replaced. Applications, including operating systems, firmware, middleware and in-house software, must avoid code specific to one address family. The RFC describes two ways to IPv6-enable an application: separate IPv4 and IPv6 logic, or combined logic that works whichever version the network uses. It recommends full functionality, scalability and security testing, plus training, because a perceived training gap makes many organisations falter. Operational tools such as monitoring and address management also need assessing, since IPv6 addresses are larger and nodes often hold two or more addresses.

For routing, IS-IS, OSPFv3 and RIPng all support IPv6, and the choice is mostly dictated by existing operational policy. The address plan starts from the advice that IPv6 addresses need not be conserved: one larger allocation is more conservative than several small blocks because it uses a single routing table entry. Each site should get at least a /48, the data center should use a /64 per VLAN, all user access networks should be a /64, and point-to-point links where NDP is not used may use a /127. Prefixes longer than /64 on network segments break functions such as SLAAC. The enterprise chooses between Provider-Aggregated space, which implies renumbering when changing ISP, and Provider-Independent space, which can ease multihoming. Delegated DNS zones need assignments on nibble boundaries such as /64, /60, /56 and /48.

For end systems, SLAAC is simple, but stateful DHCPv6 lets administrators log which system had which address, much as in IPv4, although DHCPv6 hosts are identified by a DUID rather than a MAC address. SLAAC is not recommended for servers.
sections.eli5: Before moving house you count your boxes, check what fits, and draw a floor plan. Here the boxes are devices and programs, and the floor plan is how addresses are handed out.

sections.title: IPv6 Security Myths and Real Differences
sections.content:
The RFC stresses that IPv6 is no more secure than IPv4. A new protocol has undiscovered implementation bugs, and the lack of operational security expertise is called the biggest threat. It rejects three myths. A /64 cannot be safely hidden by size, because attackers can find targets in other ways, such as enumerating DNS names. IPv6 does not mandate IPsec everywhere: RFC 6434 says IPsec support is not mandatory. And amplification attacks still exist without broadcast, because ICMPv6 messages can be generated in response to multicast, so their rate must be limited.

Many IPv4 attacks carry over: application attacks, rogue devices and flooding. ULAs and private IPv4 addresses provide no security by magic, so the edge router must filter them in both directions, and anti-bogon and anti-spoofing filtering are still needed. Differences to plan for include privacy extension addresses, which complicate audit trails; extension headers, which can defeat stateless filters; fragmentation done only by the source host, which means ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages must not be filtered; and Neighbor Discovery, which has no inherent message authentication. Enterprises that use DHCPv4 snooping should use RA-Guard and related source address validation techniques for IPv6.

In a dual-stack network the attack surface doubles, so each protocol needs a congruent security policy. For example, permitting TCP ports 80 and 443 to web servers and denying everything else must be done for both IPv4 and IPv6.
sections.eli5: A new lock is not automatically a stronger lock. You still have to check every door and window, and now there are two sets of doors, the old kind and the new kind.

sections.title: The External Phase
sections.content:
The External Phase covers how the organisation connects to the outside world: connectivity, security, monitoring and Internet-facing services. Native IPv6 from the provider is preferred as the most robust and efficient option. If that is not possible, transition tunnels can be used, but they add latency and may cause MTU problems, so the IPv4 and IPv6 MTUs should ideally match and Path MTU Discovery should work. With Provider-Independent space the enterprise may need to inject its prefix into BGP itself, unless the upstream ISP does it.

For security, filtering and monitoring matter most. Policies must be consistent between IPv4 and IPv6, with certain ICMPv6 messages allowed through, namely Packet Too Big, Parameter Problem and Time Exceeded, and Neighbor Discovery messages needed locally. The edge router should apply anti-spoofing filtering as in BCP 38. Monitoring should treat IPv6 like IPv4, and external services should be monitored per address family so that a failure of either version is noticed.

For servers, the ideal is native dual stack everywhere. As a stepping stone, operators have used NAT64 to translate inbound IPv6 connections into IPv4, which is easy but hides all IPv6 users behind one IPv4 address, or a server load balancer acting as an application proxy, which keeps native IPv6 through the security devices and can pass the client IPv6 address in an HTTP X-Forward-For header.
sections.eli5: This is fixing the front door and the mailbox first, so visitors from the new address system can reach the shop. Guards at the door must check both old and new visitors equally.

sections.title: The Internal Phase
sections.content:
The Internal Phase brings IPv6 to network devices, end-user devices and corporate systems under the design paradigm dual stack when you can, tunnel when you must. Dual stack gives a more robust, production-quality network than internal transition tunnels, which are harder to troubleshoot and may cause scalability and performance problems.

Existing IPv4 security policies must be extended to IPv6, including RA-Guard at the access layer. For first-hop router redundancy, Neighbor Discovery by default detects a router failure in 38 seconds, while VRRPv3 can switch to a backup router in around three seconds with default parameters. The choice between SLAAC and DHCPv6 depends on policy: SLAAC for ease and speed on workstations, DHCPv6 for precise control and DNS integration. RAs are still needed in DHCPv6 networks because there is no DHCPv6 default gateway option.

Operating systems differ in whether IPv6 or its privacy extensions are on by default, and some enable transition tunneling mechanisms that should be administratively shut down unless required. IPv6 should be deployed and secured at the network and infrastructure level before being exposed to end users. For corporate systems such as email, VoIP, DNS and RADIUS, DNS is a main anchor because hosts decide whether to use IPv6 by the presence of AAAA records; add them only when every service on that host name is ready.
sections.eli5: Now the rooms inside get updated one by one. Wires and shelves go first, then the people's computers, and the signpost (the name list) is changed last, once each room is really ready.

sections.title: Going IPv6-Only and Special Cases
sections.content:
Early enterprise deployments are dual stack, but the long-term roadmap should include simplifying operations by deprecating IPv4 within the dual-stack network. In some extreme cases a very large enterprise may find the address space of RFC 1918 too small, leaving IPv6-only as the only way to grow. An IPv6-only node that must reach IPv4-only nodes needs translation. The RFC points to the translation framework in RFC 6144, stateless translation in RFC 6145, stateful NAT64 in RFC 6146 and DNS64 in RFC 6147, and cautions that these have limits: NAT64 as defined translates only TCP, UDP and ICMP unicast, and the classic NAT problem of IP literals in application payloads remains. As more content is available over IPv6, less traffic needs translation.

The RFC also touches on specific enterprises. A CDN used by an enterprise should support IPv4 and IPv6 traffic selection. University campuses, which often have native IPv6 from their research and education network, commonly start with external-facing services, the computer science department and the eduroam wireless network. The Security Considerations section simply refers back to the security discussion in each phase.
sections.eli5: One day the old address language could be switched off entirely. Until then, a translator stands between the two groups, and the fewer people who still speak only the old language, the less the translator has to do.

items.title: Preparation and Assessment
items.text: Program planning, inventory, training, security policy, routing, address plan and tools. Highly recommended for all.

items.title: External Phase
items.text: Connectivity, security, monitoring and Internet-facing servers and applications.

items.title: Internal Phase
items.text: Security, network infrastructure, end-user devices and corporate systems.
